strengths: Novel framework explicitly characterizing when Gaussian universality breaks down in high-dimensional ERM through the elegant criterion: x⊤θ̂ is Gaussian if and only if the projection x⊤μ* is Gaussian
Rigorous mathematical development with careful distinction between three types of universality (performance, score, minimizer), providing valuable conceptual clarity to the landscape
Broad applicability across general convex losses, correlated non-Gaussian data with concentration properties, and smooth strongly convex regularizers—exceeding prior work in scope

Comprehensive and honest treatment of assumptions: conditional results are clearly delineated, unproven claims (Claim 4.1 on non-Gaussian CGMT, Assumption 4 on minimizer universality) are explicitly acknowledged as conjectures/assumptions
Successfully recovers fixed-point equations from RMT, AMP, and prior CGMT work, validating the framework and demonstrating its unifying power
Exceptional presentation with clear motivation (compelling examples in Figures 1-2), excellent organization (Table 1 survey), and comprehensive appendices containing full proofs

Actionable insights including: (i) performance universality can hold despite score non-Gaussianity (ridge regression), (ii) covariance-adjusted confinement reveals non-trivial geometric effects, (iii) identification of sources of non-Gaussianity in test scores
Real-data validation on MNIST demonstrating that moment-matching fails in practice, enhancing practical relevance beyond toy examples
weaknesses: Core results (Theorems 4.3, 4.4) critically depend on unproven Claim 4.1 (generalized CGMT for non-Gaussian designs), presented as conjecture. While natural and transparent, this is a foundational limitation affecting reproducibility and certainty of main claims

Theorem 6.1's characterization of universality breakdown requires unproven Assumption 4 (minimizer universality). Authors note proof is 'under preparation' but not available for review—this is a significant gap that substantially strengthens the paper if resolved

Performance universality results are limited in scope: only rigorously established for squared loss (Section 5); for general losses requires assuming score universality or asymptotic Gaussianity, substantially narrowing practical applicability

Inapplicable to non-smooth penalties (excludes Lasso and related methods) and requires smooth regularizers with bounded third derivatives (Assumption 3), limiting scope compared to modern machine learning

Limited empirical validation: only two experiments (synthetic bimodal data, MNIST) with no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported. Additional real datasets and losses would strengthen claims

Presentation is technically dense with heavy notation (Moreau envelopes, proximal operators, tensor spectral norms) that limits accessibility to practitioners. Intuition for why the non-Gaussian CGMT extension should hold is underdeveloped

Incomplete reproducibility: promised code not yet available; experimental details sparse (number of trials, computational cost, parameter sensitivity analysis missing); theoretical reproducibility depends on unproven assumptions
The practical scope of results is constrained to the proportional regime (p = Θ(n)) with convex losses only—neural networks and other non-convex settings excluded
